subject: ela
description: Students adapt how they speak to fit a variety of contexts, audiences, and tasks, and they recognize when a situation calls for formal English and when informal, conversational speech is acceptable. They judge whether a speaker's word choice, tone, and level of formality match the audience and purpose, identify slang, contractions, and casual phrasing that should be replaced in a formal setting, and revise a casual statement into appropriate formal English (or relax an overly stiff statement) so that the speech suits the occasion.
subSkills: Distinguish formal English from informal or casual speech by features such as slang, contractions, fillers, and conversational phrasing
Determine whether a given context, audience, or task calls for formal or informal speech
Judge whether a speaker's tone and word choice match the audience and purpose
Revise a casual or slang statement into appropriate formal English without changing its meaning
Recognize when overly stiff or formal speech is mismatched to a relaxed context and adjust accordingly
Explain why a particular level of formality fits or fails to fit a stated situation

problemArchetypes.name: Identify the level of formality
problemArchetypes.example: A single quoted statement is given (for example, a student saying 'Yeah, the whole thing was super cool and stuff'). The item asks whether the speech is formal or informal, with the answer signaled by clear features such as slang and fillers.

problemArchetypes.name: Match speech to context
problemArchetypes.example: A short scenario names an audience and purpose (a student presenting research to the school board). The item asks which of four spoken statements best fits that formal context.

problemArchetypes.name: Spot the mismatch
problemArchetypes.example: A brief passage describes a student giving a formal classroom presentation but using slang and casual asides. The item asks which phrase is out of place for the context and why.

problemArchetypes.name: Revise casual to formal
problemArchetypes.example: A casual sentence is given (for example, 'We kinda figured the experiment was a flop'). The item asks which revision states the same idea in appropriate formal English.

problemArchetypes.name: Evaluate and justify the best adaptation
problemArchetypes.example: A fuller scenario presents a speaker who must address two different audiences in turn. The item asks the student to evaluate which adjustment in tone and word choice best suits each audience and to justify the choice.

stimulusRules.selfContained: Every item must embed the full scenario, quoted statement, or short passage it depends on directly in the item text. The student needs nothing external: no live speech, no audio, no separate recording. The speaker's exact words and the context (audience, setting, purpose) are described in words within the item.

passageLengthByDifficulty.easy: 1 to 2 sentences: a single quoted statement, or a short statement plus a one-line description of the setting.
passageLengthByDifficulty.medium: 3 to 5 sentences describing a speaking scenario with a stated audience and purpose plus one statement to evaluate or revise.
passageLengthByDifficulty.hard: 5 to 8 sentences describing a fuller scenario, sometimes with two audiences, two competing versions of a statement, or a sequence of remarks to compare and judge for fit.

stimulusRules.noMath: No calculation of any kind is required. Numbers may appear only as harmless context inside a quoted statement.

Easy.description: Identify-level tasks from a 1 to 2 sentence stimulus. Student recognizes whether a statement is formal or informal, or picks the obviously appropriate choice, when the signal (slang, contractions, fillers) is direct and the distractors are clearly mismatched.
constraints: Stimulus is 1 to 2 sentences or a single quoted statement
Task verb is identify, name, or label
Formality cues are obvious and surface-level (clear slang, fillers, or plainly formal diction)
Only one option fits; wrong options are obviously the wrong register
No inference about competing audiences required

Medium.description: Analyze-level tasks from a 3 to 5 sentence scenario. Student matches speech to a stated context, spots a single mismatched phrase, or selects the correct formal revision, requiring inference about how tone connects to audience and purpose.
constraints: Stimulus is 3 to 5 sentences with a stated audience and purpose
Task verb is analyze, determine which fits, or revise
Two options are partially plausible, requiring the student to reason about register and meaning
Revisions must preserve the original meaning while changing formality

Hard.description: Evaluate-level tasks from a 5 to 8 sentence scenario. Student judges which adaptation best fits, compares two audiences or two versions of a statement, or diagnoses a register problem and selects the justified improvement.
constraints: Stimulus is 5 to 8 sentences, possibly with two audiences or two competing versions
Task verb is evaluate, compare, justify, or choose the best adaptation
Distractors reflect plausible but flawed reasoning about register, not obvious errors
Student must weigh formality against context and justify the judgment
May require recognizing that formal is not always better and that overly stiff speech can be a mismatch

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student believes formal English is always better, regardless of context
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reasoning that picks the most formal-sounding option for every situation, even a casual one, treating stiff diction as automatically correct rather than asking what the context calls for

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats only obvious profanity or rudeness as informal and misses slang, fillers, and contractions
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reasoning that labels a polite but slangy statement ('it was awesome and kinda wild') as formal because it is not rude, missing the casual register markers

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student judges formality by topic seriousness rather than by word choice and tone
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reasoning that calls a statement formal just because the subject is serious, ignoring the casual phrasing actually used to express it

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student changes the meaning of a statement while trying to make it formal instead of just adjusting register
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reasoning that selects a revision that sounds formal but states a different idea than the original, valuing polish over fidelity to meaning

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student assumes the same speech fits every audience and ignores who is listening
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Reasoning that chooses one statement as best for all audiences without adapting tone to the specific listener and purpose described
